intro.title: The covenants are still on our deeds
paragraphs: On Juneteenth, Barack Obama opened his presidential center in Jackson Park, on the ground where Chicago staged the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. That fair called itself the White City, and it meant it. Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass stood at its gates with a pamphlet: "The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition." Now the first Black president's words wrap a 225-foot tower on the same ground.

The two summers could not be less alike, and the contrast is the point. The fair was staged for a season of paying visitors, and its planners shut Black Americans out of its halls and its jobs. The Center was built for the people who live here, and in large part by them. That reversal did not happen on its own. For a century the neighborhoods around that park were a workshop where the tools of American housing segregation were designed, tested, and defended.

Paul Cornell bought 300 lakefront acres in 1853, cut a deal with the Illinois Central for a train stop, and sold Hyde Park to wealthy Chicagoans as a refuge from the city. Exclusivity was the product. The University of Chicago opened in 1892; the fair arrived the next summer. The promise was distance from the people who made the city run.

When Black families moved south during the Great Migration, that promise grew teeth. In 1917 the Chicago Real Estate Board adopted a policy of block-by-block segregation. In 1924 the national realtors' association wrote it into its code of ethics, barring agents from introducing anyone whose race would harm property values. In 1927 its counsel drafted the racially restrictive covenant and pushed it citywide.

Hyde Park signed up with enthusiasm. Property owners' associations went door to door; by 1928 the Hyde Park Herald bragged covenants ringed the neighborhood like a "marvelous delicately woven chain of armor." The University of Chicago spent more than $80,000 defending covenants in court. When Carl Hansberry bought near Washington Park in 1937, neighbors sued under one; his daughter Lorraine turned it into A Raisin in the Sun. The Supreme Court made covenants unenforceable in 1948. Nobody erased them. The language sits on Cook County deeds today.

Extraction found new instruments. Banks and the Federal Housing Administration had redlined Black Chicago, so Black buyers could not get mortgages. Speculators frightened white owners into selling cheap, a practice called blockbusting, then resold the same houses to Black families at double the price on contracts that built no equity and allowed eviction for one missed payment. Researchers at Duke put the losses at $3 billion to $4 billion. Woodlawn and South Shore, the blocks nearest the Obama Center, absorbed much of it.

Hyde Park chose a different tool for itself. In 1952 the university created the South East Chicago Commission to manage integration, and managing meant bulldozers. The Hyde Park-Kenwood urban renewal plan of 1958 displaced roughly 4,000 families, most of them Black and poor. James Baldwin said it plainly in 1963: "urban renewal means Negro removal."
I run Rooted Forward, a youth nonprofit that documents this history. None of it was weather. Every stage had authors, and every instrument had a signature.

The Center answers that century in kind. It was raised by Lakeside Alliance, a construction team in which four Black-owned Chicago firms hold the controlling stake, under a commitment that at least half the subcontracts go to diverse businesses. Its campus hands the park back to the neighborhood, with a new branch of the Chicago Public Library, a fruit and vegetable garden, a playground, and a sledding hill Michelle Obama asked for. The fair charged fifty cents at its gates. The Great Lawn is free, every day, to whoever walks in.

The paperwork still deserves attention. Illinois law lets homeowners record a modification repudiating racist covenant language, but few owners know it exists. Cook County should follow Edina, Minnesota, and Dane County, Wisconsin, where officials and volunteer lawyers find covenants and help residents strike them for free.

In 1893 this ground told Black Chicagoans there was no room for them in the future. On Juneteenth it said the opposite. Exclusion was engineered here. Repair is being engineered too, and this walk is a record of both.
intro.byline: Zain Zaidi is a sophomore at the University of Chicago Laboratory Schools and the founder of Rooted Forward, a youth-led nonprofit documenting Chicago's history of housing discrimination.

tour.title: Walk Hyde Park
tour.dek: A free self-guided audio tour from Paul Cornell's stone to Harper Court, told in the order it happened. Thirteen stops, about four miles, and two detours for whoever wants the rest of the story. Hyde Park sold exclusivity from its first day, and a century of paperwork decided who got to live in it.
tour.startLabel: Paul Cornell's stone, Harold Washington Park

practical.title: Getting there and timing
practical.text: The walk starts in Harold Washington Park at 53rd Street, across from the Hampton House at 5300 South Shore Drive, and ends at Harper Court, two blocks from where it began. The stops run in time order rather than in a neat loop, so the route crosses itself twice and a few stops sit within sight of each other. Plan on about three hours with the stops. The 53rd Street Metra station is a block from the start and a block from the finish. Short on time? Stop after the Obama Center, which is the halfway mark, and save the university for another day.

practical.title: The ground
practical.text: Flat city sidewalks the whole way, about four miles on the main line. The longest single leg is the sixteen minutes from the tracks down to Jackson Park. The busiest crossings are on 57th Street, along Stony Island, and at Lake Park; use the marked crosswalks. The university quadrangles are open to walk through every day. Going inside Robie House takes a timed ticket, but this tour only needs the outside.

practical.title: The two detours
practical.text: Stops twelve and thirteen sit southwest of campus, in Woodlawn, and they are drawn in green on the map because they are genuinely out of the way. The Hansberry house is where the covenant wall first cracked, and Daley's is the oldest restaurant in the city. Together they add about an hour and a half on foot. The number 63 bus and the Green Line cover the stretch if your feet are done, and the main walk is complete without them.

practical.title: Listening
practical.text: Headphones are nicest, but a phone speaker works fine. Every stop's audio is also printed on the page, so you can read instead of listen. If you share your location, it is used only to draw your dot on the map. It never leaves your phone.

stops.title: Paul Cornell's stone
stops.dek: A boulder in the grass marks where the whole neighborhood started
transcript: Find the boulder in Harold Washington Park near 53rd Street, across from the tall brick building with the red awning. That building matters in a few minutes. The stone marks roughly where Hyde Park began, and before the story starts, take one slow look around. The towers, the park, the trains behind the trees. All of it traces back to a single land deal.

One thing to know before you set off. This walk runs in the order the history happened rather than in a tidy loop, so it crosses its own path twice and a few stops sit within sight of each other. You pass 55th Street early and come back to it near the end, on purpose. The point is to watch the neighborhood get built, and then watch what got built on top of it.

Paul Cornell was a young lawyer from upstate New York who reached Chicago in 1847 with a dollar and fifty cents in his pocket, and a thief relieved him of his belongings his very first night in town. He rebuilt from nothing, and along the way he met Stephen Douglas, the Illinois senator, who gave him a piece of advice. Invest south of the city, because that is where Chicago is going to grow. So one day Cornell got on a horse and rode down the lake shore, through marsh grass and sand ridges, until he reached a small farm and tavern near what is now 53rd Street, a stopping place for travelers making the last push into the city.

In August 1853 he bought **sixty acres from Electa Watson Garnsey**, the tavern keeper's widow, and he kept buying until he held about **300 acres of lakefront** between roughly 51st and 55th. Then he gave it a name that promised gentility. Hyde Park. Chicago at the time pumped its sewage into the river and the lake and smelled like it. What Cornell was selling was escape, clean air and cool water for families rich enough to leave the city behind.

The whole plan depended on getting those families here, so in 1856 Cornell handed the Illinois Central sixty acres of his land for free. In exchange the railroad built him a **station at 53rd Street and guaranteed daily trains downtown**. The first run, on June 1, 1856, carried what the station agent wired downtown as nary a passenger up or down. Regular service started that July anyway, four trains a day at a fare of seven and a half cents, and the bet paid off so completely that by 1929 this line ran more than five hundred trains a day. Cornell cut the land into large lots, eighteen to a block with fifty feet of frontage, and kept the pace deliberately rural. Early buyers kept gardens, stables, even a few animals.

Right here on the shore he raised the resort's centerpiece, the **Hyde Park House**, a hotel with the water at its porch and the trains at its back. It hosted concerts, parties, and political dinners, and Mary Todd Lincoln stayed there for two and a half months after her husband was killed. It burned in 1877, and a generation later this stretch of shore got the Sisson Hotel, the brick tower in front of you, known today as the Hampton House.

Now look east, because the geography has been edited. The water is a few minutes' walk from here, and it did not use to be. The Hyde Park Historical Society puts it bluntly. If you had stood in 1858 where 53rd Street now meets South Shore Drive, your feet would have been wet. A breakwater ran north from that corner to make a small harbor. When the Sisson opened in 1918 the beach still started just across a narrow lakefront street. **Everything east of you now is manufactured ground.** The City Council approved filling the south lakefront in 1919, following Burnham's plan of 1909, and Chicago voters put twenty million dollars behind it in February 1920. Crews began dumping fill at 12th Street and worked south, reaching 55th by 1924. The road laid on top opened in 1929 as Leif Erickson Drive and was renamed Lake Shore Drive in 1946. If you want the old shoreline, look for the tennis courts. The water used to stop about there.

The Sisson deserves one more minute, because the pretty tower made an ugly promise. Its builder, **Harry Sisson, advertised that his guests would never encounter a Black person** under his roof, and hired no Black staff. In the 1920s, when the Klan ran openly in Hyde Park and printed its weekly paper on 55th Street, Sisson hosted a reception for the Klan's Imperial Wizard. A Catholic weekly over on 52nd Street started publishing local members' names, the chapter collapsed, and Sisson's trade collapsed with it. He sold, and the hotel changed names. Remember him when you admire the architecture on this walk. Cornell built a place that chose its neighbors, and for a hundred years, choosing kept meaning the same thing.

stops.title: The Del Prado
stops.dek: The resort era's front porch still stands on its corner
transcript: The apartment tower on this corner opened in 1918 as the **Cooper-Carlton Hotel**. Look up and you can see carved faces in the terra cotta near the top, put there by owners who claimed a family line back to the novelist James Fenimore Cooper. In 1930 it took the name **Del Prado**, inherited from an older hotel out on the Midway that was being torn down to make room for International House. You reach that older hotel's ground at stop six.

Hyde Park in these decades ran as a resort, and this corner was its front porch. Families checked in for the whole summer. They took big suites, sometimes a whole floor. The men rode Cornell's trains downtown to their offices every morning, and everyone else had the day. The beach, the parks, sailing off the Point, restaurants, concerts in the hotel ballrooms. Remember that this was the time before air travel. When people wanted to get away, they traveled close to home, and the railroads sold the getaway hard.

That sales pitch reached a long way. The Illinois Central's main line does not end downtown. Follow it the other direction and it runs through the whole length of Mississippi, and its ads told families across the Midwest and the South to come spend the summer by the lake in Chicago. The train was the only fast way anywhere, and Hyde Park sat right on it.

The building is apartments now, restored inside. Step into the lobby and look up at the ceilings, or study the arches from the sidewalk and picture check-in day in July. Trunks stacked on the curb, porters hauling a season's worth of luggage, a band playing somewhere upstairs.

Before you walk on, hold one detail. The families on this porch were white. So were the names on every deed along the boulevards. The people hauling the trunks and cooking the meals often were not, and Hyde Park's own small Black community lived two blocks west, pressed against the railroad embankment. That street is the next stop.

stops.title: The tracks and Lake Park
stops.dek: The railroad that built the resort ran both directions
transcript: These tracks are why everything else on this walk exists. Cornell's deal put a station at 53rd Street in 1856, and suburban trains have stopped here ever since, a hundred and seventy years without a break. The Illinois Central electrified the line in 1926, after the city ordered its four hundred daily coal-burning engines cleaned up, and Metra runs the same embankment today. We tend to picture this railroad as a shuttle between Hyde Park and downtown. It never was. The main line keeps going south, through the small towns of Mississippi, all the way to New Orleans.

During the **Great Migration** that geography changed America. Black southerners rode the Illinois Central north in two great waves, the first around the World Wars, the second after, hundreds of thousands of people moving toward factory jobs and away from the terror of the South. The Chicago Defender, the city's great Black newspaper, rode the same rails south in the porters' bags, telling readers to leave what it called the land of suffering. Many stepped off IC trains within a few miles of where you are standing. They built this city's industry with their hands. And nearly every neighborhood in the city, this one very much included, refused to let them live in it.

Which brings us to the street you are on. Lake Park Avenue was the working back of Cornell's stage set. The strip along the tracks fell under railroad jurisdiction, outside the village's dry laws, so this is where the saloons went. In one year in the 1870s the village issued forty-nine saloon licenses and turned down exactly one. Add the coal yards, the liveries, and the cheap frame buildings, and you have the unglamorous machinery that kept a resort running.

It is also where Hyde Park put its Black neighbors. In the early 1900s a small **middle-class Black community lived along Lake Park and Harper avenues**, close against the tracks. There was an AME church on Lake Park, a colored Republican Club, and a social column in the Defender. The 1900 census along this street lists the Black cooks and waiters who staffed the hotels, most of them born in Kentucky, Tennessee, and Mississippi, boarding next to white pipe welders and Chinese laundry owners. In 1914 the neighborhood's Half Century Club held a reception at the Rosalie Music Hall for Booker T. Washington, the most famous Black man in America. Meanwhile the rest of Hyde Park stayed almost entirely white, and worked to keep itself that way.

Stand here a second and read the pattern, because it repeats all afternoon. The front door on the boulevards, the Black community beside the tracks. Geography doing the work of policy, decades before the policy got written down. The next four stops are about what Hyde Park was selling, and then you meet the paperwork.

stops.title: The White City
stops.dek: The parks came first, and then the fair that drew the hardest line of all
transcript: You are in Jackson Park, and the domed building across the water is the last of the great palaces of the **1893 World's Columbian Exposition** still standing where the fair put it. Everyone remembers the fair. Almost nobody remembers that the park came first, and that the park is the only reason the fair could happen here at all. So start with the ground.

Paul Cornell spent two decades trying to will great parks into existence on this end of the city. He and his allies began pushing a parks bill in 1866, voters turned the first one down, and Cornell rode to Springfield two winters running to fight for the next. The act passed on **February 24, 1869**, and the commissioners it created went looking for ground. They picked out **1,055 acres** of sand bar, bog, and open water six miles south of downtown, including everything around you, and hired the two men who had just built Central Park, **Frederick Law Olmsted and Calvert Vaux**.
What those two drew in 1871 is on this page, and it is worth a minute of your time. One park on the lake, one park a mile west, and a green channel joining them.

Read the table in the left margin, because the plan counts itself out. The whole thing came to 1,055 acres, split into an Upper Division of **372**, a Midway Division of **90**, and a Lower or Lagoon Division of **593**. The Upper Division is Washington Park, and it is still 372 acres. The Lagoon Division is where you are standing. The Midway Division is the strip that connects them, and Olmsted meant to run **water down the middle of it**, so a boat could come in off Lake Michigan, cross the lagoon here, and tie up at a landing in Washington Park. The sheet promises fourteen miles of drives, thirty miles of walks, and a mile and six tenths of frontage on the lake. Neither park had a name yet. They were divisions of one South Park until the commission asked the public for suggestions and settled on Jackson and Washington in 1881.

Two things in the report make the ground vivid. Olmsted opened by complaining that the site's first obvious defect was its flatness, and he described this end as a built-up sand bar, made by the lake throwing sand at itself for centuries. And on the whole thousand acres, he counted **not more than a dozen small dwellings**. Washington Park got built more or less as drawn, including a hundred acres of turf called the Southopen Green where sheep were kept on to crop the grass. Jackson Park did not.

The Great Fire of October 1871 burned the drawings, and it burned the county land records the commission's condemnation cases depended on. The money went to rebuilding the city. A designer named Horace Cleveland was brought in the next year to do what could still be afforded, which meant paths and planting rather than the enormous excavation the water plan needed. Washington Park filled in over the next two decades. This end stayed rough ground, sketched as a garden and never made into one, and that is exactly why the fair chose it. When Chicago beat New York, Washington, and St. Louis for the World's Fair, the planners needed hundreds of open lakefront acres, already publicly owned, close to rail lines. Daniel Burnham looked at Jackson Park's emptiness and saw a blank page. Olmsted, by then an old man, came back to shape the ground he had planned a generation earlier, and pulled the Wooded Island out of the sandbar. Land prices around the site started climbing the moment the decision was announced.

Put the fair in scale. The last great exposition, in Paris, had produced the Eiffel Tower. Chicago, barely twenty years past its fire, meant to answer it. Burnham directed an army of architects who threw up a city of palaces in about two years, and they look like carved stone in the photographs. They were mostly **steel frames skinned in plaster**, and the fastest way to make them match was paint. The painters chose a single white, and the newspapers did the rest. The White City. At night it was lit with electricity on a scale almost nobody had seen, and the crowds came as much for the glow as for the exhibits.

It ran from the first of May to the end of October and drew some **27 million visits, in a country of 65 million people**. One October day alone brought 761,000 through the gates. Visitors met the dishwasher, the zipper, Juicy Fruit gum, and a wheel built by a bridge engineer named Ferris. The fair also planted a lie that would outlive it. A food company hired **Nancy Green, a Chicago woman born into slavery in Kentucky**, to flip pancakes in costume as Aunt Jemima, a smiling plantation cook invented to sell flour. The image charmed the crowds and sold the Old South as a warm memory, at the exact moment the fair was doing something colder.

Because Black Americans were shut out of this fair. Shut out of its planning, its exhibit halls, and nearly all of its jobs. **Ida B. Wells and Frederick Douglass** answered from the gates with a pamphlet, The Reason Why the Colored American Is Not in the World's Columbian Exposition, printed with prefaces in English, French, and German so any visitor on earth could read it. Wells counted the copies she handed out in the thousands. Douglass, then in his seventies, worked from the Haiti Pavilion, the one building where Black excellence was on display, because Haiti, not America, had made him its commissioner. The fair's answer was a single Colored American Day, late in the summer. Douglass gave the speech of the summer anyway.

Then the White City burned. A January 1894 fire took the Casino, the Peristyle, and the Music Hall, and killed a firefighter named William Mackie. On the evening of July 5, at the height of the Pullman strike, a fire near the Terminal Station took seven of the great buildings in one night while about a hundred thousand people came to watch. The Tribune blamed boys playing in the ruins. Almost everything that did not burn was dismantled and carted away. The domed palace in front of you survived for one unglamorous reason. It held borrowed art, and the lenders had demanded a fireproof building, so **Charles Atwood built it on a brick and steel frame** and only skinned it in plaster like the rest.

So here is what is actually left, and it is more than most people think. That building spent the 1930s being rebuilt in about 28,000 tons of Indiana limestone, cut to copy Atwood's original detail, and it has been a science museum since 1933. It took the name **Kenneth C. Griffin Museum of Science and Industry** in 2024. The water in front of it is the Columbia Basin, the last piece of the fair's north lagoon, and the arched bridge across it was renamed for Clarence Darrow in 1957 and has been fenced shut since 2013 while the city works out how to rebuild it. South of the basin, Olmsted's Wooded Island is still there. Japan gave the fair a temple pavilion called the **Ho-o-den** on that island, and it outlived the fair by fifty years, until it was boarded up after Pearl Harbor and burned by arsonists in 1946. A Japanese garden went back in 1981, took the name Osaka Garden in 1993, and in 2016 Yoko Ono set twelve steel lotus petals on the spot where the pavilion stood.

One more, at the south end of the park. **The Statue of the Republic** still stands where the fair's Administration Building was, though what you see is a 24-foot bronze that Daniel Chester French cast in 1918, a third the size of the gilded plaster original that the park commissioners deliberately burned in 1896. Right now she is inside scaffolding, being regilded for the first time since 1992. That work is being paid for as one of the conditions attached to building the Obama Presidential Center in this park, which is the next stop, about ten minutes south. Keep the pamphlet's title with you as you go. The fair asked this neighborhood a question it never answered honestly, which is who all of it was actually for.

stops.title: The Obama Center
stops.dek: The one place where this walk steps out of order, on purpose
transcript: This walk runs in time order, and this stop breaks it. Everything from here on happens before 2026. You are standing here now because the answer belongs beside the question, and the question was asked a quarter mile north, across the water, in 1893.

Stand on the plaza where you can see the whole tower. Near the top, the granite wall turns into carved letters, lines from the speech Barack Obama gave at Selma in 2015. The museum opened on **June 19, 2026. Juneteenth.** It took almost five years to build, cost about 850 million dollars, and the Obamas chose this park, this exact ground, where Chicago staged the fair you just walked away from. There is a lineage in that choice. The blocks around you launched Harold Washington, the city's first Black mayor, and Carol Moseley Braun, the first Black woman in the United States Senate, before they launched a president.

Hold the two summers side by side, because the contrast is the whole point of this tour. The White City went up fast, for one season of ticketed crowds, and its planners kept Black Americans out of its halls and out of its jobs. This tower was raised by **Lakeside Alliance, a construction team in which four Black-owned Chicago firms hold the controlling stake**, with a pledge that at least half the subcontracts go to diverse businesses. And where the fair was fenced, this is a park. Around you sit a **new branch of the Chicago Public Library**, a fruit and vegetable garden, a playground, and a hill built for winter sledding because Michelle Obama asked for one. The people the fair kept out are the people this place was made for.

The Center also put money back into the ground it sits on. The federal review that cleared construction came with conditions, and those conditions are why the Golden Lady is in scaffolding this summer getting her first regilding since 1992, why the century-old comfort station out on Marquette Drive is being rebuilt, and why the park has to tell its own history to visitors. A building that arrived in 2026 is paying to repair things the fair left behind in 1893.

Now the walk goes back in time. Everything from here is how the neighborhood behind you actually got built, and who was kept out of it while it was being built. It starts a few hundred yards west, with a hotel that opened the same spring as the fair.

stops.title: The first Del Prado
stops.dek: A fair hotel's ground became the university's front door to the world
transcript: The Gothic tower facing the Midway is International House, and under it lies the hotel that gave stop two its name. In April 1893, with the fair about to open, a buff brick hotel called the **Raymond and Whitcomb Grand** was rushed to completion right here. Four stories, 325 rooms, another 62 in an annex, and its best feature ran the full length of the building. A **250-foot verandah facing the Midway**, so guests could take breakfast watching the strangest street on earth. It soon took a grander name, the Del Prado.

The fair minted hotels like this all along the neighborhood's edges. The Del Prado, the Chicago Beach, the Windermere, all opened for 1893 with wonders the guests wrote home about. Hot and cold running water, steam heat, electric light, telephones. The Illinois Central raised its tracks onto the embankment you crossed earlier just to move the crowds, an estimated four million riders in one summer. When the fair ended, the hotels stayed, and for a generation this stretch ran as one of the most famous resort hotel districts in the country.

It did not last. By 1930 the Del Prado was, in one writer's words, worn and tired, its great verandah long since enclosed. The university bought the ground, pulled the hotel down, and raised **International House**, a residence built with Rockefeller money to board students from around the world. Its name moved up to 53rd Street, where the Cooper-Carlton wears it still.

Notice what happened on this block, because it happens again and again on the ground ahead of you. A neighborhood institution ages, the university buys the land, and something in Gothic stone replaces it. In the decades to come the university would absorb the Piccadilly, the Broadview, and the Shoreland the same way. There is a real irony in the particular swap made here. The hotel had been a private pleasure palace for white travelers. The house that replaced it was built so students from around the world could live under one roof, in a neighborhood that was at that very moment sealing itself shut against Black Chicagoans a mile west. Both things are true on this ground. Hold them both, and walk on west down the Midway.

stops.title: The Midway line
stops.dek: A canal that never came, and a border that did
transcript: This mile of green was the fair's pleasure strip. The White City down the lawn to the east was the exhibition, dignified and ticketed. Out here was the fun. Beer gardens, bands, sideshows, restaurants from a dozen countries, and rising over the middle of it the first **Ferris wheel**, 264 feet tall, America's answer to the Eiffel Tower. Fifty cents bought two slow revolutions, about twenty minutes in the air. The shows out here took in millions, and every carnival midway in America has been named for this lawn ever since. The wheel outlived the fair by only a little. Crews spent 86 days taking it apart, it limped through two more engagements, and its company went bankrupt while Ferris himself died young in 1896.

It had a darker draw too. The Midway's so-called villages put human beings on display, people brought from Africa, Asia, the Middle East, and the Americas, presented under the banner of anthropology for paying crowds who stared at them like exhibits. The Tribune recommended the exhibit as a chance to descend the spiral of evolution. That happened here, on this grass, and the fair sold tickets to it all summer.

Now look at the ground itself. You saw the reason on the 1871 plan two stops back. The lawn sits sunken below the streets because **Olmsted meant to dig a canal here**, water linking the Jackson Park lagoons to Washington Park a mile west. Crews started digging, the money ran out, and the water never came. The ditch stayed a lawn.

But the empty channel found another job. **The Midway became a border.** North of this grass, the university and white Hyde Park. South of it, Woodlawn. And when the Great Migration filled the Black Belt to bursting, that narrow strip of housing along State Street, now flanked by the Dan Ryan, families started looking for rooms anywhere they could find them. The blocks south of the Midway were the pressure line. For most of a century, which side of this lawn you lived on decided your mortgage, your rent, and what the city thought your block was worth. The numbers stayed blunt for decades. As late as 1980, the blocks just northeast of here ran about 86 percent white, and the blocks northwest of campus about 88 percent Black. Cross the lawn today and you can still feel the seam.

That line was not drawn by accident, and it was not drawn by geography. It was drawn on paper, by people with names, and the next four stops introduce them one at a time. A mile southwest of here, in 1937, a family named **Hansberry** bought a brick three-flat across one of those paper lines, and a mob gathered outside their window the first evening. Their daughter Lorraine grew up to put that year on Broadway as A Raisin in the Sun. Their house is stop twelve, an optional detour, and the paperwork that brought the mob is explained there, standing in front of the building it was written against.

stops.title: Rockefeller Chapel
stops.dek: The tallest building on campus stands where houses used to
transcript: This is Rockefeller Chapel, finished in 1928, and it is still the tallest thing the university owns. That is not an accident. When John D. Rockefeller made his final gift to the school he had bankrolled, he asked that a chapel be its **central and dominant feature**, so that anyone looking at the skyline would read the university's priorities in stone. The architect, Bertram Goodhue, gave it a 207-foot tower, and a later Rockefeller filled that tower with one of the largest carillons on earth, 72 bells cast in England.

Now look at the photograph from the year it rose. At the bottom edge of the construction site you can see houses coming down. Building the chapel meant **demolishing a row of homes on Woodlawn Avenue**, and the chapel was only one project among many. Between 1926 and 1933 the campus nearly doubled, twenty-one new Gothic buildings, and the land under them had rarely been empty. The university was becoming the biggest landowner on the South Side one block at a time, and it had learned to buy quietly, once even parking a title under its own architect's name so sellers would not know who was assembling the ground.

Keep that habit in mind, because this walk keeps meeting it. A chapel takes a row of houses in 1928. Veterans' prefabs fill the Midway in 1946. A forty-one-acre campus expansion pushes south of the Midway in the 1950s, over the objections of the families living there. Hospitals take more blocks in the 1990s and 2000s. None of these projects was evil on its face, and some were genuinely good. The point is simpler. For a century, when this institution needed ground, it got the ground. The people on it moved. The last two stops of this walk are what happened when that power was turned on a whole neighborhood at once.

stops.title: The Robie House
stops.dek: What the professors' quarter built when money was no object
transcript: Frederick Robie made bicycle parts. He ran his father's supply company, he was twenty-eight, and in 1908 he went to **Frank Lloyd Wright** with an engineer's brief. No boxy rooms, no drafts, and he wanted to see his neighbors without his neighbors seeing him. By 1910 he had this. Long Roman brick, roofs that hang far past their walls, a house that seems to be gliding while standing still. Wright called the style Prairie. Plenty of the neighbors just called it strange.

For this walk, though, the house is really about money, and about the street it sits on. When the university opened in 1892, the blocks around it filled with big houses for professors, deans, and executives, many built on lots bought from Marshall Field himself. Woodlawn Avenue became the street where the money showed. Walk a block in either direction after this stop and look at the porches and the stonework. Hiring the most radical architect in America was simply what this street could afford, and it is exactly the class of resident Paul Cornell had imagined from the beginning.

The house itself was nearly lost twice. The seminary next door announced demolition in 1941, and a letter campaign saved it. It tried again in 1957, and this time the rescue came from an unexpected direction. Wright, ninety years old, declared it the finest house he ever designed, Carl Sandburg compared the wreckers to book burners, and the man who actually wrote the check was **William Zeckendorf**, the developer who at that moment was rebuilding 55th Street on cleared urban renewal land, a story this walk reaches at the end. He bought the house, used it as his site office, and passed it to the university. The man profiting most from the neighborhood's demolition saved its most famous house. Today it is a World Heritage Site.

Now hold the two halves of this block in your head at once, because this is where the machinery gets assembled. Money confident enough to build this house was also confident enough to write rules about who could never own one. In **1909, one year after Robie hired Wright**, a Hyde Park lawyer founded a club on these blocks whose stated purpose was keeping Black families out. That club is the first tool in the kit, and the red plate below is how it worked. The second tool is at the next stop, and it turned this neighborhood's habit into a national profession's rulebook.

interrupts.title: The improvement associations
body: An improvement association was **a homeowners' club organized to control who could live on its blocks**. The clubs came before the paperwork, and this neighborhood built the prototype. In **August 1909** a Hyde Park attorney named Francis Harper organized the **Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club**, 350 members strong, with a stated mission of maintaining the color line. Its targets were not newcomers. Black doctors, teachers, and shopkeepers had lived in Hyde Park for fifteen years. The club pledged to **blacklist any realtor who sold to a Black buyer**, to buy out Black homeowners, and to replace Black workers with whites. A decade on, the neighborhood's Property Owners' Journal was still putting the theory plainly. **"Every colored man who moves into Hyde Park knows that he is damaging his white neighbors' property. Therefore, he is making war on the white man."** The educator Fannie Barrier Williams, a Hyde Parker of fifteen years, answered for her neighbors. "I've lived here for 15 years. What you trying to drive me out of my community?"

Where the paper failed, dynamite followed. Between **1917 and 1921 white Chicagoans bombed more than fifty Black homes** and the offices of the Black banker **Jesse Binga**, who kept writing mortgages anyway and told the papers, "If they can make me move, they will say, we made Jesse Binga move. No, I will not run." Of the forty bombed families, two moved. In 1918 Baltimore's mayor wrote his realty board about "a plan they have" in Chicago for keeping Black families out of white blocks. Around the country, the association method became known simply as **the Chicago plan**.

stops.title: Cobb Hall and the quad
stops.dek: A brand new university dressed up to look five hundred years old
transcript: The building in front of you, with the pointed arch over its doors, is **Cobb Hall, the university's first building**. Classes started inside it on October 1, 1892, with 594 students, while the fair's palaces were still going up a mile east. It was paid for by Silas Cobb, a Chicago harness maker who had arrived nearly penniless sixty years earlier, and designed by an architect named Henry Ives Cobb. No relation. The university simply had that kind of luck with names.

This is actually Chicago's second University of Chicago. The first was a Baptist school founded in the 1850s a few miles north, at 35th and Cottage Grove, on ten acres donated by Senator Stephen Douglas. The same Douglas who tipped off Paul Cornell, and a man whose fortune ran partly on a Mississippi plantation worked by enslaved people. That first school went bankrupt in 1886. When the Baptists set out to build a successor, they aimed much higher. **John D. Rockefeller pledged $600,000**, on the condition that others raise $400,000 more, and Marshall Field, the department store king, put in the first ten acres of land right here. Rockefeller's gifts eventually passed $35 million, and a seminary project became one of the richest universities on earth.

Now look hard at the architecture, because the architecture is a confession. Everything around you was brand new in the 1890s, but the trustees ordered **English Gothic, modeled on Oxford and Cambridge**, precisely so the campus would look like it had stood for five centuries. They planted ivy at the feet of the walls to hurry the illusion along. A new school in a new city bought itself instant ancestry.

The university's relationship to its neighbors was more complicated than its walls suggest. In 1942 it hired **William Allison Davis, the first Black scholar to hold full faculty rank at a majority-white American university**, with a Rosenwald grant paying his salary. Then it let the neighborhood it had helped seal shut do the rest. Davis and his family could not rent in Hyde Park or Kenwood. One of the most distinguished professors on this quad went home at night to Washington Park, on the far side of a line his own employer had helped pay to defend. The faculty club denied him membership for years. The ivy caught up with the walls in a few seasons, and the university's welcome took a good deal longer.

It is worth being exact about what stopped him, because it was not a mood. Every landlord and agent in this neighborhood was working inside a written rule, and the rule was written by a trade association three miles up Michigan Avenue. The red plate below is that rule.

One more thing before you move on. To make its name fast, the young university bet on football. It was a founding member of the conference that became the Big Ten, and its coach, Amos Alonzo Stagg, was the first in America hired with faculty rank. The team practiced on the Midway just south of this quad and played in a stadium one block north of here. That stadium is the next stop, and so is the experiment that ended up underneath its stands.

interrupts.title: The realtors' rulebook
body: The word **Realtor** is not a job. It is a membership, coined in 1916 and owned by a trade association, and for twenty-six years that association's written ethics made selling a house to a Black family in a white neighborhood a punishable offense. On **June 6, 1924**, at its seventeenth annual convention, the **National Association of Real Estate Boards adopted Article 34** of its Code of Ethics. **"A Realtor should never be instrumental in introducing into a neighborhood a character of property or occupancy, members of any race or nationality, or any individuals whose presence will clearly be detrimental to property values in that neighborhood."** The back of that booklet gives the association's address. **310 South Michigan Avenue, Chicago.** The national rule was written three miles from where you are standing.

It had teeth. The association's bylaws required every member board to adopt the code, and any board that would not enforce it could be expelled. A NAREB model licensing act, taken up by **32 states**, let state commissions pull an agent's license for a code violation, which turned a private club rule into something close to state law. The local board had already gone first. In **1917 the Chicago Real Estate Board** set up a Special Committee on Negro Housing and adopted a policy of filling the city **block by block**, insisting it was "dealing with a financial business proposition and not with racial prejudice." Board members from Hyde Park, Kenwood, and Oakland lobbied the city for outright racial zoning, warning of a quarter of a billion dollars in lost property value, and were stopped only because the Supreme Court had just struck racial zoning down. On **May 4, 1921** the Chicago board voted to expel any member who sold to a Black buyer on an all-white block.

The appraisal textbooks taught the same thing as arithmetic. **Frederick Babcock's 1924 Appraisal of Real Estate** told students on page 71 that "residential values are affected by racial and religious factors," listed a district's "racial movements" among the routine data an appraiser should gather, and printed a worked example in which Black arrival is simply written up as the cause of decline. Babcock joined the **Federal Housing Administration in 1934** and ran its underwriting division, and the government's 1938 manual repeated his doctrine almost word for word.

The race language came out of the code in **1950**, two years after the Supreme Court made covenants unenforceable. The euphemism it left behind, about property "detrimental to property values," stayed until **1974**. Black brokers, shut out of membership all along, had built their own association in **1947** and called themselves Realtists, under the motto Democracy in Housing. On **November 19, 2020**, the association's president Charlie Oppler apologized for the whole history. "We can't go back to fix the mistakes of the past," he said, "but we can look at this problem squarely in the eye."

stops.title: Stagg Field and the pile
stops.dek: Football crowds, then the atomic age, on one city block
transcript: Stand at the bronze. The block behind it, all the way east to University Avenue, was **Stagg Field**. The stadium looked like a castle, with notched stone walls and round towers, and on big fall Saturdays crowds pressing fifty thousand poured off the trains and into these streets to watch the Maroons, one of the first powers of college football. The 1905 team went unbeaten and outscored its opponents 271 to 5. Football fame is what first made this university a household name. The photograph on this page shows the field about 1900, before the permanent stands went up, with the quadrangles you just walked standing behind it.

Then the university fired its own myth. **Robert Maynard Hutchins**, the young president who arrived in 1929, thought big-time sports had no business at a serious university, and in December 1939 he abolished varsity football outright. Chicago walked out of the Big Ten a few years later. Understand what that cost, because you will watch the bill come due at the end of this walk. Alumni walked away and took their checkbooks. Undergraduate enrollment collapsed from about five thousand to about twelve hundred, applications fell by more than half, and the university started eating its endowment to stay open. Hutchins built a different identity instead, the great-books Core that still shapes every undergraduate here, and on race he settled for half measures, quietly tolerating the covenants his own faculty called repulsive. A broke university convinced its neighborhood was the problem is where the wreckers on 55th Street came from.

The emptied stadium then got the twentieth century's most consequential second act. In 1942 the Manhattan Project was building its first reactor out in a forest preserve southwest of the city, precisely because the experiment was so dangerous. Then a builders' strike stalled the site, and rather than wait, Enrico Fermi convinced his chiefs he could run it safely in a **squash court under the west stands of the empty stadium**, a room thirty feet by sixty with a balcony at one end. On the afternoon of December 2, 1942, his team slid the control rods out of a pile of graphite and uranium and ran the **first self-sustaining nuclear chain reaction in history**. It went critical at 3:25 in the afternoon and Fermi shut it down twenty-eight minutes later, in secret, in a residential neighborhood of a city of more than three million people. Even the mayor was never told.

So look around, because almost all of it is gone and the markers are precise about where things were. The castle came down in 1957. **Henry Moore's Nuclear Energy went up on this exact spot on December 2, 1967, twenty-five years to the day**, about twelve feet of bronze on a granite plaza. Moore said the top is both a mushroom cloud and the dome of a skull, and that underneath it is architectural, with arched cavities like the inside of a cathedral. Walk around it. From the north it is a mushroom cloud. From the south you are looking into a crypt. The federal government made this the Site of the First Self-Sustaining Nuclear Reaction, a National Historic Landmark, and the plaques are set into the plaza at your feet.

Behind the sculpture is the **Regenstein Library**, ribbed concrete, finished in 1970 on the old playing field. Beside it is the low glass dome of the **Mansueto Library**, opened in 2011, which holds three and a half million books in a robotic vault fifty feet underground. Physics made this university's name global, and the buildings that mark it are libraries. But while its scientists were remaking the world, its lawyers and planners were remaking the neighborhood, and that story finishes this walk.

stops.title: The Hansberry house
stops.dek: One family's move into this three-flat cracked the covenant wall
transcript: You have left the tour's main line to get here, and it is worth saying why this address earned the walk. At first glance it is a brick three-flat on a quiet Woodlawn block. In 1937 it became one of the most important buildings in the legal fight against housing segregation in America, and the little girl who lived behind that window grew up to put what happened here on Broadway.

**Carl Hansberry** came up from Mississippi in the Great Migration, one of the hundreds of thousands the Defender called north. He became a real estate broker, and he watched his people pay double for half. The paper wall this walk has been tracing ran right through here. These twelve blocks are the **Washington Park Subdivision**, built on the ground where the Washington Park Race Track ran until Illinois shut down horse racing, one street south of the park itself. Its covenant was signed on **September 30, 1927** and recorded that February, it barred owners from selling or leasing to any Black buyer except live-in servants, and it was written to run until the first day of 1948. It was also the very covenant the University of Chicago had helped defend in court four years before Hansberry arrived. He chose the block deliberately. He wrote later, in the Defender, "I figured the most vulnerable spot to attack the restrictive covenants was where the pressure was the greatest."

In the spring of 1937 he bought this building and moved in his family. A white mob gathered. Something came through the window, a brick by some accounts, a chunk of concrete by others, and it barely missed the head of his seven-year-old daughter, **Lorraine**. A neighbor named Anna Lee sued to enforce the covenant, and the case, **Hansberry v. Lee**, went all the way to the Supreme Court. The weak point was in the paper itself. The covenant only took effect if the owners of **95 percent of the frontage** signed it, an earlier case had been settled on everyone simply agreeing that they had, and the Hansberrys' lawyers showed the real number fell well short. In 1940 the family won, on the ground that they could not be bound by a judgment reached in a case where nobody had represented them. It was a technicality rather than a ruling on covenants themselves, but it voided the paper on this neighborhood, and the Defender reported that it opened hundreds of homes to Black Chicagoans. The wall did not fall for eight more years. This is where it cracked.

The honest version of Carl Hansberry is complicated, and this tour owes it to him. He fought the covenants, sued a railroad over segregated cars, printed know-your-rights pamphlets, and founded a business league to bankroll Black enterprise. He also made part of his fortune carving buildings into cramped kitchenettes, the same one-room conversions this tour describes at 55th Street. City officials called the family slumlords while inspectors buried them in fines. The Black press called him a race man. Both were describing the same cage from different sides, a market where a Black landlord could sell his people nothing better because the city allowed nothing better. Worn down and disillusioned, he was preparing a move to Mexico when he died there in 1946.

Lorraine carried this house with her. In 1959 her play **A Raisin in the Sun**, about a Black family deciding whether to move into a white neighborhood that does not want them, became the first play by a Black woman produced on Broadway. The mob outside these windows is in it. So is the arithmetic of the kitchenettes. It opened while the bulldozers this walk ends with were already rolling, and a letter writer to the Defender in 1962 caught the whole century in one line. If the bomb doesn't get him, the bulldozer will.

interrupts.title: Restrictive covenants
body: A racial covenant was **a ban written into a property deed**, a clause in which the owner promised never to sell or rent to a Black person. It bound every later owner of the land, so one signing campaign could seal a block for generations. Through the 1910s the idea spread quietly, and in **1926 the Supreme Court, in Corrigan v. Buckley, let covenants stand** because they were private contracts between neighbors. That was the green light.

In **1927 the Chicago Real Estate Board circulated a model covenant**, drafted by the national association's counsel Nathan William MacChesney, and pushed it block by block through churches, clubs, and property owners' associations. The model text is worth reading once, because it says out loud what the century said quietly. **"No part of said premises shall in any manner be used or occupied directly or indirectly by any negro or negroes,"** with an exemption for janitors, chauffeurs, and house servants actually employed on the property. More than **220 Cook County subdivisions** adopted the language, one study counted **40 square miles of Chicago** under covenant, and by 1925 a realtor could brag to the Hyde Park Herald that the covenants ringing that neighborhood were **"like marvelous delicately woven chain armor."**

The University of Chicago helped pay for the armor. It gave money to the **Hyde Park Protective Club** to spread covenants on the blocks around campus, quietly financed the 1933 lawsuit that kept Black families out of the blocks near Washington Park, and spent **$83,597 defending covenants in court**, over the objection of its own sociologist Louis Wirth, who called them morally repulsive. The covenant on the building in front of you came out of that campaign.

When **Carl Hansberry bought at 6140 South Rhodes** in 1937 anyway, a chunk of concrete thrown through the window nearly hit seven-year-old Lorraine. The Supreme Court let the family stay in **1940** on a technicality, and in **1948, in Shelley v. Kraemer, it made every racial covenant in America unenforceable**. Nobody erased them. The words still sit on Cook County deeds today, including on deeds a few blocks from here.

stops.title: Daley's Restaurant
stops.dek: The oldest restaurant in Chicago has watched this whole story from one corner
transcript: In 1892 an Irish immigrant ironworker named **John Daley opened a lunchroom here at 63rd and Cottage Grove**, feeding the crews building the elevated railroad above the street, with the World's Fair rising a mile east. That makes it, by most accounts, **the oldest restaurant in Chicago**, older than the L trains it fed. In 1918 Daley sold to two Greek immigrants who worked in the place, a waiter named Tom Kyros and a cook named Paul Emmanuel, and the same extended family has run it ever since. They kept the Daley name. It was already worth something.

Think about what has passed this corner since. 63rd Street became one of the busiest commercial streets in Black Chicago as the Great Migration remade Woodlawn, and the restaurant stayed put and fed its neighborhood while so much else moved away or burned. The menu turned toward smothered pork chops, catfish, and biscuits because that is what the neighborhood wanted. **Muhammad Ali ate here between training sessions** in the 1960s. Disinvestment hit 63rd as hard as any street in the city, the L overhead was even torn back, and Daley's kept the griddle on. In 2019 it moved into a new building directly across the street, at 6257 South Cottage Grove, and kept serving.

A restaurant is a small thing to set against covenants and bulldozers. But notice what it proves. A business that stayed, served whoever walked in, and changed with its neighbors instead of fleeing them has outlived nearly every business in this story. Get the breakfast. Then head back north, because the last two stops are where the story you have been following gets finished with heavy equipment.

stops.title: Fifty-Fifth Street
stops.dek: When the covenants fell, the speculators arrived
transcript: In 1948 the Supreme Court made racial covenants unenforceable, and Hyde Park's paper wall came down. After decades boxed inside the overcrowded Black Belt, Black families could finally buy on blocks like this one, and they did. In 1940 Hyde Park was one and a half percent nonwhite. By 1956 it was almost thirty-seven percent, with twenty thousand white residents leaving and twenty-four thousand Black residents arriving in six years. What met them was not a welcome. It was a business, and it worked the block rather than the house.

Hyde Park fought that business harder than most neighborhoods did, and mostly with volunteers. More than sixty **block clubs** formed at the peak, and they reported illegal conversions, met the panic calls at the front door, sat with owners who were being worked on, and on at least one block quietly **passed the hat so a Black family trapped in a punitive contract could keep their home**. They were arguing against arithmetic, though, and the arithmetic had been written into federal policy a decade earlier.

The same arc had already run once, a mile northwest of here, and every mansion owner in the city knew it. **Drexel Boulevard** was laid out on the ruins of a dream called Egandale, four hundred acres a doctor drained and enclosed for grand gardens that never got built. The parkway cut through it became the most exclusive boulevard on the South Side, castles and chateaux behind formal plantings, with the oldest public fountain in Chicago anchoring its foot. Then the elevated train arrived in 1909, the wealthy drifted north, and the mansions were cut into flats, six units becoming twelve becoming thirty-six. The color line settled into the alley behind Cottage Grove, one block over. When the money left, it took the boulevard's name off the society pages, and decades of redlining and disinvestment did the rest. The fountain still runs. Walk Drexel today and you can read this whole tour in one street.

The crowding was part of the machine too. Buildings that started as fair-era hotels and one-family flats were carved into **kitchenettes**, single rooms with a hot plate and a shared bathroom down the hall. More tenants meant more rent from the same walls. Then the crowding and the wear were pointed at as proof that Black neighbors ruined property, by the very interests collecting the rents.

Now picture this street before any of the concrete around you existed. Dozens of bars, clubs, and shops ran along 55th and Lake Park, the tavern count climbing every year the covenants aged. The Compass Players opened in a storefront at 1152 East 55th in 1955, the troupe that grew into Second City. It was crowded, loud, newly integrated, a little rough, and more alive than almost any street in the city.

The university two blocks south looked at all that life and saw a threat to its future, and it had the legal power to act on the thought. Everything you can see from this corner is what replaced 55th Street. The twin concrete slabs on their island in the middle of the road are **I. M. Pei's University Apartments**, 540 units finished in 1961, with closed-circuit television at the doors and the street split around them to keep traffic slow. The low rows behind their fenced front courts went up at the same time. A working commercial street of small buildings and small rents became a planned one of large buildings and larger ones. Who decided that, and what it cost, is the last stop of this walk.

interrupts.title: Blockbusting
body: Blockbusting was **the business of turning white panic into profit**. The speculator's opening move was fear at the dinner hour, **phone calls night after night and flyers under every door**, telling white owners a Black family had bought on the block and their equity was about to vanish. A house worth **$15,000 went for $14,000** to the speculator. Within days the same house sold to a Black family for **$27,000, on contract**, because the redlined banks had left them no other way to buy.

The trade depended on **both prejudices at once**. It needed white owners who believed a Black neighbor destroyed value, and it needed Black buyers desperate enough to pay double for what the city refused to sell them honestly. The white seller lost, the Black buyer paid brutally, and the man in the middle kept the difference. It turned over block after block of the South Side in a few short years.

interrupts.title: Redlining
body: Redlining was **the color-coding of neighborhoods by race, for the purpose of lending**. In 1939 and 1940 a federal agency, the **Home Owners' Loan Corporation**, graded every Chicago neighborhood for mortgage risk. Green was best, then blue, then yellow, then red. The grades were not invented in Washington. **Local realtors and lenders filled out the surveys**, men trained on the industry's race-based appraisal manuals, and the government inked their judgments onto maps. As few as **three or four Black families could get a whole neighborhood stamped hazardous**. Most of the Black Belt was drawn red. Hyde Park and Kenwood were drawn yellow, definitely declining, in part because Black Chicago lived next door.

The **Federal Housing Administration** pointed lenders the same way. Its 1938 underwriting manual, written under the same **Frederick Babcock** whose appraisal textbook you met two stops back, told appraisers to investigate whether **"incompatible racial and social groups"** were present and warned that a neighborhood keeps its value only if it keeps the same racial occupancy. The same manual listed the deed restrictions it wanted to see, including **"prohibition of the occupancy of properties except by the race for which they are intended."** A red or yellow grade meant no ordinary mortgage, no home improvement loan, and no business loan, for every address on the block at once. When the NAACP pressed Franklin Roosevelt to act, the answer that came back, as the historians in The Shame of Chicago retell it, was that this was the market, and the market had to be respected.

The results were absolute. When the Black realtor **Dempsey Travis** led a survey of Chicago's 243 white-owned banks, **exactly one would lend to a Black family moving into a white neighborhood**. Hyde Parkers eventually built their own answer, a **savings and loan raised in 1952 from 750 small donors** so Black neighbors could get ordinary mortgages and rehab loans. Everywhere else, the banks left a vacuum, and somebody was always waiting to fill it.

interrupts.title: Buying on contract
body: A contract sale was **rent with none of rent's protections, dressed up as ownership**. The buyer put money down and paid monthly, but **owned nothing until the final payment**. Miss one month and the seller could evict, keep every dollar already paid, and sell the house again on a fresh contract. Researchers at Duke found that **75 to 95 percent of the homes sold to Black families in 1950s and 60s Chicago were sold on contract**, at an average markup of **84 percent**. A city commission study of one just-changed neighborhood found 82 percent of sales to Black families were on contract at nearly twice the home's value. The sellers were often syndicates of downtown professionals, and the financing came from **the same banks that had refused the buyers a mortgage**.

The lawyer **Mark Satter** spent the 1950s dragging the scheme into the light after two clients, Sally and Albert Bolton, paid faithfully for two years, went late once, and got an eviction notice. He found they had paid **three times what their seller had**, and he spent the rest of his short life naming the operators, writing that banking policy and "the wicked speculators exacted a fearful tribute from the Negro man and his family." He died at forty-nine, and the Daily News wrote that he fought the money lenders when other lawyers shied away.

The buyers finally beat the system themselves. In the late 1960s, families on the West Side organized the **Contract Buyers League**, confronted their sellers together, and held payments in escrow like a rent strike through the coldest days of January 1970. **Over 400 contracts were renegotiated**, worth about six million dollars back then. The Duke study put the total wealth taken from Black Chicago families through contract sales at **$3.2 to $4 billion**.

interrupts.title: Urban renewal
body: Urban renewal was **the legal power to declare blocks blighted, clear them with public money, and choose what replaced them**. The **Hyde Park-Kenwood plan, approved November 7, 1958, was the nation's first large federally supported renewal scheme**, driven by the university's **South East Chicago Commission**, and Illinois's 1953 conservation law, which the university helped write, went further, letting planners condemn blocks that only **might decline someday**. The cleared land cost the public about **$40 million and was resold to developers for $4 million**.

What it built is the street you are standing on, the townhouses, the mid-street towers, the shopping court two blocks north. What it removed was the housing poor families could afford and **641 businesses**, from the bars and taverns of 55th Street to the corner hardware store. Nearly **4,000 dwelling units came down and about 2,100 went up**, priced for a different class of neighbor. The university opposed public housing in the plan area, and **only 34 units were ever built**. Planners called it conservation. The tools changed over the century, from a club to a code of ethics to a deed clause to a color on a map to a wrecking ball. **The incentives never did.**

stops.title: Harper Court
stops.dek: The last stop is two blocks from the first one, and that is the point
transcript: You are two blocks from Cornell's boulder, a hundred and seventy years later, and this corner is where the story lands. Start with why the wreckers came. By 1950 the university was in real trouble. The Hutchins reforms you heard about at the stadium had cut undergraduate enrollment to about twelve hundred, the endowment was draining, and the trustees seriously discussed moving the whole institution out of Chicago. They stayed for the plainest of reasons. Nobody buys a used campus. So the new president, Lawrence Kimpton, drew the other conclusion. If the university could not leave the neighborhood, the neighborhood would have to change. In 1952, after the wife of a faculty member was kidnapped from her home and a thousand residents packed a protest meeting, the university created the **South East Chicago Commission** and handed it to a lawyer named Julian Levi. Levi ran it for almost thirty years and described it himself, in a university publication, as the political wing of the university.

Levi helped write the state and federal renewal laws he needed, then used them. An Illinois law the university lobbied through Springfield in 1953 went further than anything before it. A private body could now target blocks that merely **might become blighted**. One of the first areas so designated sat right by campus, where the residents were largely Japanese American families, many of them resettled from wartime internment camps, and Black families whose buildings were, by their own block clubs' accounting, in good shape. St. Clair Drake, the Black sociologist who co-wrote Black Metropolis, lived there and joined the lawsuit against the plan. It went ahead anyway. Hyde Park and Kenwood became the site of the **first great federally backed urban renewal scheme in the country**.

The mechanics were blunt. Blocks were declared blighted. Public money bought them by eminent domain and cleared them. Demolition started along 55th and Lake Park in 1955, and the full plan passed City Council in 1958. By the summer of 1962, 564 of the 856 buildings marked for demolition were already down. When it was over, nearly **four thousand dwelling units were gone and about twenty-one hundred had replaced them**, and close to **twenty thousand people had been displaced**. Under the final plan, the great majority of displaced families were Black. Of the families steered into subsidized housing, 484 were Black and 15 were white. The neighborhood lost more than a quarter of its population in the 1960s alone. James Baldwin, watching the same program at work in San Francisco, gave it the name that stuck. Urban renewal, he said, "means Negro removal." Planners had a different phrase, and in 1958 the comedians Mike Nichols and Elaine May tried out a joke about it at a Hyde Park fundraiser. Here we stand, black and white, shoulder to shoulder, against the lower classes. The Herald reported nervous laughter.

Look at the two photographs taken from the same spot on the tracks in 1955 and 1961. That is a working commercial street becoming a shopping center with a parking lot. **641 businesses disappeared** in the clearance. Renting families got moving money. Renting businesses got nothing. Anderson Hardware was pushed off 55th three separate times, and once, when the notice came too fast, its customers loaded the stock into shopping carts and moved the store themselves. What could rebuild was what a mortgage would approve, and the mortgage wanted chains. Woolworth, Walgreens, a candy shop, a burger bar. Jane Jacobs was writing The Death and Life of Great American Cities at that exact moment and used Hyde Park as a warning, a neighborhood surrendered to a single landlord's idea of order.

This particular corner is the gentler part of the story. When the wreckers took the 57th Street art colony, the shacks left over from the 1893 fair that had housed Chicago's bohemia for half a century, neighbors raised money, took Small Business Administration loans, and built **Harper Court** in 1965 to rehouse the displaced artisans at rents under a hundred dollars. The old cast-iron horse trough from the colony came along as a planter. It worked for a generation, became the neighborhood's living room, and then the university-backed redevelopment of the 2000s tore that down too, for the glass tower above you.

Two things are true at once about what happened here, and the honest version of this tour holds both. Hyde Park after renewal became one of the few Chicago neighborhoods where integration more or less held, roughly a third Black and half white for decades, and residents who fought for that outcome meant it. The Herald called it worth whatever price must be paid. And the price was paid mostly by people who never got a vote, in a plan built on the theory, stated almost openly, that integration was acceptable so long as the poor were removed. In 1962 students sat in at the administration building for two weeks after proving, with paired Black and white test couples, that the university was refusing Black tenants in its own apartment buildings. The chairman of the campus chapter that ran the test was a twenty-year-old named Bernie Sanders. The university negotiated an end to the sit-in and, in time, the policy.

So run the whole line once before you go. Cornell buys the marsh and picks his buyers. Olmsted draws the parks and the fire burns the drawings. The fair dazzles the world while Wells and Douglass hand out the truth at its gates. The professors' quarter starts a club, the realtors write it into their ethics, their lawyer drafts the deed clause, the government colors the maps, the speculators write the contracts, and the bulldozers finish the job. Every stage had authors who signed their names. None of it just happened, which means none of it has to keep happening. That is the whole argument of this walk. Thanks for going the distance with us. The rest of Rooted Forward's work lives at rooted-forward.org.
